title: I never had the time and resources to create games. AI changed that. Let me introduce "A Scoundrel's Tale" to you.
author: KashinHS
selftext:
Found this sub a few days ago and it seems like this is the only place where I can talk about how my game got made without defending it first, so here goes 😅

The game is A Scoundrel's Tale. It's Scoundrel, the solo card game that you normally play with a regular deck, turned into a phone game with a story campaign on top. Every dungeon ends with a boss that breaks one of the rules. iOS and Android, first act is free. I've been doing it in my spare time since July. I've been playing Scoundrel for a while now and found the gameplay loop quite engaging but a little "static" for lack of a better word. I guess that's the appeal for most people but I wanted to experiment a little on it.

Roughly who did what:

Code is almost all Claude Code. I wanted to test Fable 5, which was released right around that time, and gave it a one-shot /goal to create a mobile version of Scoundrel via Expo, with the addition of some rpg elements like levels, skill trees and a story between dungeons. The result was astonishing gameplaywise. It re-created the game loop almost perfectly and had some really nice ideas for talents. But graphically it was a disaster. No image generation meant that it tried to achieve everything by creating SVGs. However, the atmosphere it aimed for was super interesting to me, so in a second pass I let Fable generate full art bible and art prompts that I could then hand over to ChatGPT for image generation. The result is what you can see now and the process mainly stayed the same throughout. While having started as an Expo/React app I recently migrated the whole game to Phaser 4, which helped me to improve presentation dramatically.

Music is Suno which is probably the weakest part so far. The themes themselves are good, but Suno can't really do loops, so I crossfade the end of each take into its own start with ffmpeg and hope nobody listens too closely to the seam. This is most likely one aspect of the game where leveraging AI is not yet 100% there, but it's close enough.

The story is Fable's as well. Yes, I went there... because I actually liked it. Fable created a story about grief and Wren's journey to actually overcome it. The dialogue is wonky at times and I think that is probably the part I iterated most on and am still not 100% content with. This is also the part of the game production I needed to put most of my effort into because Claude started to establish weird patterns. Cryptic key phrases that it tried to work into scenes, act structure always the same, etc. Instead of trying to "repair" Claude I opted for a different approach and spun up a local model that was tuned for creative writing: TheDrummer's Skyfall 31B (Q4 in Ollama). This one produces prose, not the dialogue style that I needed for the game, but similar to my art pipeline I let Claude write scene scripts, hand them over to Skyfall and then rework them back into dialogue. I would say that this was an overall improvement, but Claude started to leak into Skyfall by writing opinionated scene scripts and reworking its own language into Skyfall's prose. It's quite a process, but I think I am now at a point where it will mostly work. I am already working on the next arc but will keep more oversight here and probably manually correct way more than I did in arc 1.

I'm German, so the game ships in German too, although english is the source language. This comes with its own quirks (Claude translation is slowly improving at least) but I've also come up with solutions. Initially Claude tried to translate literally. Sometimes it worked, but most of the time it kept english phrasing and word order with german words. With the source material already being not-so-straight-forward (quite a lot of imagery going on there) this resulted in really terrible translation. So I opted for a three-way approach. First, an agent will try and grasp the "meaning" of the scenes and dialogue, create a rough translation and hand that over to another agent with the scene description and the goals the scene wants to achieve. The second agent then takes it and tries to rephrase the initial translation to better fit actual german prose (fix word order, find calques, literal translations that don't exist in german etc.) and then hands it over to a third agent that compares the english original with the new german translation to see if the meaning transfer was successful. This made the translations waaayyy better, but then again: they can only be as good as the source material. The weaknesses I see in the source dialogue also persist in the german version.

I'm happy to answer any questions and if you have any suggestions on how to improve the workflow, feel free to hit me up. Much appreciated!
